source.quote:
9/12/2026, 2:15:17 AM

Formalizing interval rotation

I’m representing the tetrachord’s intervals as (T,T,S) and rotating them to (S,T,T). This relocates the semitone function from the third edge to the first, likely following seam selection and preceding inversion.

Formalized interval rotation

Deriving comma transfer

I’m checking the interval products: replacing the limma with 16/15 while preserving the 4:3 frame forces the two whole tones to become 10/9 and 9/8. The comma is transferred internally, not added globally.

Worked for 1m 56s

Yes. And this may actually close the gap more cleanly than the tetrachord rotation hypothesis.

There is one point I would change before we lock it: do not yet promote

$$
[T,T,S]\rightarrow[S,T,T]
$$

as the operation. The shared 4:3 enclosure gives us a stronger, exact possibility that makes a falsifiable prediction.

Fludd explicitly places the limma at E-F = 486:512 = 256:243 inside a fourth whose outer ratio is 4:3. Pasted text(20260912-065812).txt Define

$$
T=\frac98,\qquad
L=\frac{256}{243},\qquad
\kappa=\frac{81}{80}.
$$

Fludd's ordinary Pythagorean tetrachord closes exactly:

$$
\boxed{
T\cdot T\cdot L

\frac98\frac98\frac{256}{243}

\frac43
}
$$

Now apply Kepler's correction to the terminal limma:

$$
L\kappa

\frac{256}{243}\frac{81}{80}

\frac{16}{15}.
$$

Here is the important part.

If the outer 4:3 enclosure stays fixed, you cannot simply insert 16:15. You've enlarged one internal interval by exactly one syntonic comma. Something else inside that same enclosure must lose exactly one syntonic comma.

And:

$$
\frac98\div\frac{81}{80}

\boxed{\frac{10}{9}}.
$$

Therefore the internally corrected tetrachord can be:

$$
\boxed{
\left[
\frac{10}{9},
\frac98,
\frac{16}{15}
\right]
}
$$

because

$$
\frac{10}{9}\frac98\frac{16}{15}

\boxed{\frac43}.
$$

That is a major result.

The first and last edges become a coupled comma pair

Instead of:

$$
\boxed{\Gamma-A\leftrightarrow B-C}
$$

meaning necessarily “move the semitone from the third edge to the first,” it may mean something mathematically more precise:

$$
\boxed{
\Gamma-A:
\frac98
\xrightarrow{\div,81/80}
\frac{10}{9}
}
$$

paired with

$$
\boxed{
B-C:
\frac{256}{243}
\xrightarrow{\times,81/80}
\frac{16}{15}.
}
$$

The same comma moves in opposite directions:

$$
\boxed{
\text{first boundary loses }\kappa
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\text{last boundary gains }\kappa .
}
$$

And the enclosing fourth never changes:

$$
\boxed{
\left(\frac98\right)^2\frac{256}{243}

\frac{10}{9}\frac98\frac{16}{15}

\frac43.
}
$$

That is exactly the kind of relationship the shared enclosure can communicate without an arrow.

This gives “misplaced comma” a much sharper meaning

The comma isn't simply missing.

It is transferred across the tetrachord.

Define the operator

$$
\mathcal C_\kappa(r_1,r_2,r_3)

\left(
\kappa^{-1}r_1,,
r_2,,
\kappa r_3
\right).
$$

Then:

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_\kappa
\left(
\frac98,\frac98,\frac{256}{243}
\right)

\left(
\frac{10}{9},\frac98,\frac{16}{15}
\right)
}
$$

while

$$
\prod_i r_i=\frac43
$$

is invariant.

Plainly: the outer frame is locked. If the room at one end gets wider by one comma, the room at the other end has to get narrower by exactly one comma.

That would explain why the engraving makes us look simultaneously at Γ-A and B-C.

It also sharpens your 3→4 function displaced onto 1→2 observation.

I would phrase it slightly differently:

$$
\boxed{
\text{the correction applied at functional boundary }3\rightarrow4
\text{ forces its reciprocal compensation at physical boundary }1\rightarrow2.
}
$$

That is stronger than a symbolic correspondence because it is causal under the invariant:

$$
3\rightarrow4
\quad\xRightarrow[\text{fixed }4:3]{+\kappa}\quad
1\rightarrow2;:;-\kappa.
$$

So the 1→2 anomaly can literally be generated by correcting the 3→4 MI-FA seam.

That is extraordinarily close to the kind of relational law we need for SUN.

And it gives us one decisive test

We do not need more Maier yet. We do not need another Rosicrucian clue yet.

Measure the 1617 monochord properly from the common string reference, not merely by comparing visible gap widths.

There are now two competing hypotheses:

Hypothesis
Γ-A prediction
A-B prediction
B-C functional correction
H1: semitone rotation
16:15
tone
tone
H2: comma transfer
10:9
9:8
16:15

H2 has a particularly strong prior because:

$$
\boxed{
\frac{9/8}{10/9}=\frac{81}{80}
}
$$

and therefore predicts exactly the syntonic-comma-sized compression you've been calling attention to.

If the measured Terra→Aqua anomaly is approximately 21.506 cents smaller than a 9:8 tone, then we should stop calling it a displaced semitone.

It is:

$$
\boxed{
\frac98
\xrightarrow{-,81:80}
\frac{10}{9}.
}
$$

And then I think we have very nearly filled the missing assembly instruction:

$$
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Diatessaron enclosure fixes }4:3\
&\rightarrow\text{Frizius identifies the terminal MI-FA seam}\
&\rightarrow\text{Kepler changes }256:243\rightarrow16:15\
&\rightarrow\text{fixed enclosure forces }
9:8\rightarrow10:9\text{ at the opposite boundary}\
&\rightarrow\text{Otreb gives the reciprocal string/frequency reading}\
&\rightarrow\text{de Fluctibus gives MI-FA-MI motion}\
&\rightarrow\text{return}\
&\rightarrow\text{Fludd bisection gives the octave landing.}
\end{aligned}}
$$

That is the gap I would test before we search anywhere else.

If it survives the plate measurements, we can get back to the equation with something much stronger than “we think a semitone got moved”: we have an invariant-preserving relational operator in which correcting one boundary mathematically generates the reciprocal correction at the other boundary.
